Imagine a stack of plates in your 
kitchen or cafeteria .
You add new plates only on the top, 
and you remove the top plate when 
needed .
You never take a plate from the middle or 
bottom - the last plate you placed is the 
first one you take .
This is exactly how a Stack works in 
programming - the last element 
added is the first one to be removed 
(LIFO ).

text:
Basic Idea
•Stacks is a linear data structure that follows the LIFO (Last-In-First-Out) principle and allows 
insertion and deletion operations from one end of the stack data structure, that called top.
•A stack/operation is an Abstract Data Type (ADT), commonly used in most programming 
languages . It is named stack as it behaves like a real-world stack, for example - a deck of cards or 
a pile of plates, etc.
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Why Stack Algorithms ?
➢Efficient Data Management – Stacks allow Last In, First Out (LIFO) 
operations, which help manage data efficiently in recursive algorithms 
and function calls.
➢Memory Management – Used in function call stacks for managing 
memory during recursive calls, ensuring proper execution flow.
➢Expression Evaluation – Stacks help in converting infix expressions to 
postfix/prefix and evaluating postfix expressions efficiently in compilers 
and interpreters .
➢Backtracking Algorithms – Used in AI search algorithms, solving mazes, 
and navigating decision trees by storing states and backtracking when 
needed .
➢Undo/Redo Operations – Used in text editors, AI-assisted design tools, 
and web browsers to implement undo/redo functionality .Sudipta Roy, Jio Institute 5
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Why Stack Algorithms ?
➢Parsing and Syntax Checking – Stacks help in syntax validation of 
programming languages, checking balanced parentheses, and processing 
nested structures .
➢Recursion Implementation – Recursion inherently uses stacks to store 
function call information, helping in problems like Tower of Hanoi (ToH).
➢AI & ML Algorithmic Optimization – Many AI/ML algorithms, like Depth -First 
Search (DFS), use stacks for efficient traversal and exploration .
➢Real-time Data Processing – Stacks are used in stream processing, such as 
parsing real-time stock market data, event -driven simulations, and chatbot 
response handling .
➢Scheduling & Memory Allocation – Operating systems use stacks for 
managing system processes, handling function execution order, and 
optimizing memory allocation .
Sudipta Roy, Jio Institute 6
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
In various other ways in ML/DL
•Memory Management : Stacks can be used for memory management during the training 
process, especially in deep learning where large amounts of memory are required for 
storing intermediate results, gradients, and parameters .
•Function Call Stacks : In deep learning frameworks, such as TensorFlow or PyTorch , 
stacks are used to manage the execution of computational graphs . Each operation or 
layer in the neural network is added to the stack during the forward pass, and the 
gradients are computed and propagated backward during the backpropagation phase .
•Hyperparameter Tuning : Stacks can be used to implement algorithms for 
hyperparameter tuning, such as grid search or random search . Each set of 
hyperparameters is pushed onto the stack, and the performance of the corresponding 
model is evaluated .
•Model Ensemble : Stacks can be used to implement model ensemble techniques, such

•Model Ensemble : Stacks can be used to implement model ensemble techniques, such 
as stacking or blending . In stacking, predictions from multiple base models are used as 
features for a meta -model, which is trained on the stacked predictions . The meta -model is 
then used to make final predictions . Stacks can be used to store intermediate predictions 
from the base models .
•Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) : Stacks can be used to implement the recurrent 
connections in RNNs . In RNNs, the hidden states at each time step are stored in a stack 
and passed as inputs to the next time step, allowing the network to capture sequential 
dependencies in the data.

•Use an element array of MAX size to represent a 
stack. 
•Use a variable TOP to represent the index/or 
address of the top element of the stack in the 
array. It is this position from where the element 
will be added or removed 
•TOP = -1 indicates that the stack is empty
•TOP = MAX -1 indicates that the stack is full

Push Operation
•The push operation is used to insert an element into the stack. 
•The new element is added at the topmost position of the stack. 
•First check if TOP==MAX -1. 
If true, then it means the stack is full and no more insertions can further be 
added, an OVERFLOW message is printed. 
•If not true, increase TOP by 1, then add the element at TOP position

•The peek operation first checks if the stack is empty or contains 
some elements.

Algorithm to PUSH an element in a stack
Step 1: IF TOP = MAX -1, then

Step 3: SET STACK[TOP] = VALUE
Step 4: END
Algorithm to POP an element from a stack
Step 1: IF TOP = NULL, then

 Goto Step 4

Step 2: SET VAL = STACK[TOP]
Step 3: SET TOP = TOP - 1
Step 4: END

text:
The algorithm steps
1.Print operands as they arrive .
2.If the stack is empty or contains a left parenthesis on top, push the incoming operator 
onto the stack.
3.If the incoming symbol is a left parenthesis , push it on the stack.
4.If the incoming symbol is a right parenthesis , pop the stack and print the operators 
until you see a left parenthesis . Discard the pair of parentheses .
5.If the incoming symbol has higher precedence than the top of the stack, push it on 
the stack .
6.If the incoming symbol has equal precedence with the top of the stack, use 
association . If the association is left to right, pop and print the top of the stack and 
then push the incoming operator . If the association is right to left, push the incoming 
operator .
7.If the incoming symbol has lower precedence than the symbol on the top of the 
stack, pop the stack and print the top operator . Then test the incoming operator 
against the new top of stack.

Indian Wedding Invitation Chain
Imagine a traditional Indian wedding in a village where one family doesn’t send 
out printed invites but instead relies on a word -of-mouth invitation chain :
How it works :
1. Initial Invitee ( Main Function Call ):
The bride's family tells one trusted person (say, Ramesh) to inform the community.
2. Ramesh tells the next person, who tells another:
Each person takes the responsibility to inform one more — just like a function calling itself with a new 
input.
3. Stopping Point (Base Case):
The chain continues until someone reaches a person who already knows or is the last on the list — the 
base case .
4. Returning back with confirmations:
As each person finishes their task, they pass the confirmation back up the chain — just like how recursion 
"returns" values as it unwinds.
5. Chain of Communication = Call Stack:
The entire process works only because each person remembers who told them and who they informed —

simpler subparts . Second the function calls itself but with subparts

obtained by combining the solutions of simpler sub-parts.

text:
Pros and Cons of Recursion
Pros
•Recursive solutions often tend to be shorter and simpler than non-recursive ones.
•Code is clearer and easier to use. 
•Follows a divide and conquer technique to solve problems .
•In some (limited) instances, recursion may be more efficient .
Cons
•For some programmers and readers, recursion is a difficult concept . 
•Recursion is implemented using system stack. If the stack space on the system is limited, 
recursion to a deeper level will be difficult to implement . 
•Aborting a recursive process in midstream is slow. 
•Using a recursive function takes more memory and time to execute as compared to its non-
recursive counterpart . 
•It is difficult to find bugs, particularly when using global variables .

text:
N Queen Problem | Backtracking
•The N Queen is the problem of placing N chess queens on an N ×N chessboard so that no two queens 
attack each other. For example, the following is a solution for the 4 Queen problem.
Method 
1) Start in the leftmost column
2) If all queens are placed
 return true
3) Try all rows in the current column. 
 Do following for every tried row.
 a) If the queen can be placed safely in this row 
 then mark this [row, column] as part of the 
 solution and recursively check if placing
 queen here leads to a solution.
 b) If placing the queen in [row, column] leads to
 a solution then return true.
 c) If placing queen doesn't lead to a solution then
 unmark this [row, column] (Backtrack) and go to 
 step (a) to try other rows.
4) If all rows have been tried and nothing worked,
 return false to trigger backtracking.

memory allocation, making them efficient for applications where the number 
of elements varies frequently .
➢Efficient Insertions and Deletions : Insertions and deletions in linked lists 
have an average time complexity of O(1) or O(N), depending on the 
operation type, while arrays require O(N) due to shifting elements .
➢Flexible Data Storage : Linked lists efficiently handle sparse data structures 
and large-scale dynamic datasets, making them useful in AI/ML for handling 
real-time data streams .
➢Implementation of Abstract Data Types (ADTs) : Stacks, queues, graphs, 
and hash tables can be efficiently implemented using linked lists.
➢Memory Efficiency : Linked lists use only the required memory, unlike arrays, 
which may allocate excess memory even when not needed .

•Doubly linked list is almost similar to singly linked list except it contains two address or 
reference fields, where one of the address field contains reference of the next node and other 
contains reference of the previous node. 
•First and last node of a linked list contains a terminator generally a NULL value, that 
determines the start and end of the list. 
•Doubly linked list is sometimes also referred as bi-directional linked list since it allows traversal 
of nodes in both direction .
•Since doubly linked list allows the traversal of nodes in both direction, we can keep track of 
both first and last nodes .

Circular Linked List
•A circular linked list is basically a linear linked list that may be single - or double -linked .
•The only difference is that there is no any NULL value terminating the list. 
•In fact, in the list every node points to the next node and last node points to the first node, thus 
forming a circle. Since it forms a circle with no end to stop it is called as circular linked list. 
•In circular linked list there can be no starting or ending node, whole node can be traversed from 
any node. 
•In order to traverse the circular linked list, only once we need to traverse entire list until the 
starting node is not traversed again . 
•A circular linked list can be implemented using both singly linked list and doubly linked list.

text:
Backtracking
To discuss depth -first traversals, we will define a backtracking algorithm for stepping 
through a tree:
•At any node, we proceed to the first child that has not yet been visited
•Or, if we have visited all the children (of which a leaf node is a special case), we backtrack to 
the parent and repeat this decision making process
 We end once all the children
of the root are visited

text:
Why Binary Tree ?
➢Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval : Binary trees provide an efficient way to 
store and retrieve hierarchical data, such as file systems, databases, and 
organizational structures .
➢Optimized Searching and Sorting : Binary Search Trees (BSTs) allow for O(log 
n) time complexity in search operations, making them crucial for optimizing 
AI/ML algorithms .
➢Hierarchical Representation : Many real-world problems involve hierarchical 
relationships (e.g., decision trees, neural networks, knowledge graphs) that 
can be modeled using binary trees.
➢Tree Traversals for Data Processing : Different traversal methods (in-order, 
pre-order, post-order, and level-order) are used for various tasks, such as 
expression evaluation, hierarchical clustering, and syntax tree analysis .
➢Foundation for Advanced AI/ML Models : Trees are the backbone of 
advanced machine learning models like Decision Trees, Random Forests, and 
Gradient Boosting Machines (GBMs) .

Why Binary Tree ?
➢Optimal Memory Usage : Unlike arrays, binary trees dynamically allocate 
memory, making them more space -efficient for certain applications .
➢Graph -Based Problem Solving : Trees serve as the foundation for graph -
based structures, commonly used in AI for knowledge representation, 
recommendation systems, and AI search algorithms .
➢Used in AI Heuristics and Search Algorithms : Tree structures are critical for 
game theory (Minimax, Alpha -Beta pruning), AI planning, and heuristic search 
algorithms like A and Dijkstra's algorithm* .
➢Faster Data Processing in AI Pipelines : Many AI/ML pipelines use tree-based 
indexing methods like KD-Trees, Quad -Trees, and Octrees to speed up spatial 
queries and high-dimensional data searches .
➢Essential for Compiler Design and Expression Parsing : Abstract Syntax Trees 
(ASTs) are widely used in compilers and interpreters for parsing and 
executing programming languages efficiently .

# Iterative function for inorder tree traversal
def inOrder(root):
# Set current to root of binary tree
current = root
stack = [] # initialize stack
while True:
# Reach the left most Node of the current Node
if current is not None:
# Place pointer to a tree node on the stack

text:
Huffman Coding - Tree
Steps to build Huffman Tree
1.Input is an array of unique characters along with their frequency of 
occurrences and output is Huffman Tree. 
2.Create a leaf node for each unique character and build a min heap of all 
leaf nodes (Min Heap is used as a priority queue . The value of frequency 
field is used to compare two nodes in min heap . Initially, the least frequent 
character is at root)
3.Extract two nodes with the minimum frequency from the min heap .
4.Create a new internal node with a frequency equal to the sum of the two 
nodes frequencies . Make the first extracted node as its left child and the 
other extracted node as its right child. Add this node to the min heap .
5.Repeat steps# 2 and #3 until the heap contains only one node . The 
remaining node is the root node and the tree is complete .

text:
Threaded Binary Trees
Advantages of Threaded Binary Tree
•It eliminates the use of stack as it perform linear traversal, so save memory .
•Enables to find parent node without explicit use of parent pointer
•Threaded tree give forward and backward traversal of nodes by in-order 
fashion
•Nodes contain pointers to in-order predecessor and successor
•For a given node, we can easily find inorder predecessor and successor . 
So, searching is much easier .
•In threaded binary tree there is no NULL pointer present . Hence memory 
wastage in occupying NULL links is avoided .
•The threads are pointing to successor and predecessor nodes . This makes 
us to obtain predecessor and successor node of any node quickly .
•There is no need of stack while traversing the tree, because using thread 
links we can reach to previously visited nodes .
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Threaded Binary Trees
Disadvantages of Threaded Binary Tree
•Every node in threaded binary tree need extra information(extra memory) to indicate whether its 
left or right node indicated its child nodes or its inorder predecessor or successor . 
•Insertion and deletion are way more complex and time consuming than the normal one since 
both threads and ordinary links need to be maintained .
•Implementing threads for every possible node is complicated .
•Increased complexity : Implementing a threaded binary tree requires more complex algorithms 
and data structures than a regular binary tree. This can make the code harder to read and 
debug .
•Extra memory usage : In some cases, the additional pointers used to thread the tree can use up 
more memory than a regular binary tree. This is especially true if the tree is not fully balanced, 
as threading a skewed tree can result in a large number of additional pointers .

Binary Search Trees
•A binary search tree (BST), also known as an ordered binary tree, is a variant of binary 
tree in which the nodes are arranged in order . 
•In a BST, all nodes in the left sub-tree have a value less than that of the root node . 
Correspondingly, all nodes in the right sub-tree have a value either equal to or greater 
than the root node . 
•The same rule is applicable to every sub-tree in the tree. 
•Due to its efficiency in searching elements, BSTs are widely used in dictionary problems 
where the code always inserts and searches the elements that are indexed by some key 
value .

•The value of the key of the right sub-tree is greater than or equal to the value of its

# A utility class that represents an individual node in

class Node:

text:
Threaded Binary Trees
•In the linked representation of a BST, a number of nodes contain a NULL 
pointer either in their left or right fields or in both . This space that is wasted in 
storing a NULL pointer can be efficiently used to store some other useful piece 
of information. 
–For example, the NULL entries can be replaced to store a pointer to the in -order 
predecessor, or the in -order successor of the node. These special pointers are called 
threads and binary trees containing threads are called threaded trees . In the linked 
representation of a threaded binary tree, threads will be denoted using dotted lines.
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Threaded Binary Trees
•In one way threading, a thread will appear either in the right field or the left field of 
the node. 
•If the thread appears in the left field, then it points to the in -order predecessor of 
the node . Such a one way threaded tree is called a left threaded binary tree. 
•If the thread appears in the right field, then it will point to the in -order successor of 
the node . Such a one way threaded tree is called a right threaded binary tree.

text:
AVL Trees
An AVL tree is a binary search tree such that for any node in the tree, 
the height of the left and right subtrees can differ by at most 1.
–AVL is named by its inventor Adelson -Velskii and Landis
–The key advantage of using an AVL tree is that it takes O( logn) time to perform search, insertion and 
deletion operations in average case as well as worst case (because the height of the tree is limited to 
O(logn)).
–The structure of an AVL tree is same as that of a binary search tree but with a little difference. In its 
structure, it stores an additional variable called the BalanceFactor .
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
AVL Trees
–The balance factor of a node is calculated by subtracting the height of its right 
sub-tree from the height of its left sub -tree. 
 Balance factor = Height (left sub -tree) – Height (right sub -tree)
–A binary search tree in which every node has a balance factor of -1, 0 or 1 is 
said to be height balanced. 
–A node with any other balance factor greater than | 1 | is considered to 
be unbalanced and requires rebalancing.
•If the balance factor of a node is 1, then it means that the left sub -tree of the 
tree is one level higher than that of the right sub -tree. Such a tree is called 
Left-heavy tree . 
•If the balance factor of a node is 0, then it means that the height of the left sub -tree is equal to the 
height of its right sub -tree. 
•If the balance factor of a node is -1, then it means that the left sub -tree of the tree is one level lower 
than that of the right sub -tree. Such a tree is called Right -heavy tree .

39Properties
•The depth of a typical node in an AVL tree is very close to the 
optimal log N.
•Consequently, all searching operations in an AVL tree have 
logarithmic worst -case bounds .
•An update (insert or remove) in an AVL tree could destroy the 
balance . It must then be rebalanced before the operation can be 
considered complete .
•After an insertion, only nodes that are on the path from the 
insertion point to the root can have their balances altered .
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Inserting a Node in an AVL Tree
•Since an AVL tree is also a variant of binary search tree, insertion is also 
done in the same way as it is done in case of a binary search tree. 
•Like in binary search tree, the new node is always inserted as the leaf node . 
But the step of insertion is usually followed by an additional step of rotation .
•Rotation is done to restore the balance of the tree. However, if insertion 
of the new node does not disturb the balance factor, that is, if the 
balance factor of every node is still -1, 0 or 1, then rotations are not 
needed .
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Rotations to Balance AVL Trees
•To perform rotation, our first work is to find the critical node . Critical node is the nearest ancestor 
node on the path from the root to the inserted node whose balance factor is neither -1, 0 nor 1. 
•The second task is to determine which type of rotation has to be done . 
•There are four types of rebalancing rotations, and their application depends on the position of the 
inserted node with reference to the critical node . 
➢LL rotation: 
➢the new node is inserted in the left sub -tree of the left child of the critical node
➢RR rotation: 
➢the new node is inserted in the right sub -tree of the right child of the critical node
➢LR rotation: 
➢the new node is inserted in the right sub -tree of the left child of the critical node
➢RL rotation: 
➢the new node is inserted in the left sub -tree of the right child of the critical node

text:
Splay Trees
•A splay tree is a self -balancing binary search tree with an additional property that 
recently accessed elements can be re -accessed fast.
• It is said to be an efficient binary tree because it performs basic operations such as 
insertion, search and deletion operations in O(log(n)) amortized time. 
•For many non -uniform sequences of operations, splay trees perform better than 
other search trees, even when the specific pattern of the sequence is unknown.
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Splay Tree
•When a node in a splay tree is accessed, it is rotated or "splayed" to the root thereby 
changing the structure of the tree. 
•Since the most frequently accessed node is always moved closer to the starting point 
of the search (or the root node), those nodes are therefore located faster. 
•A simple idea behind it is that if an element is accessed, it is likely that it will be 
accessed again.
•In a splay tree, operations like insertion, search and deletion are combined with one 
basic operation called splaying . Splaying the tree for a particular node rearranges the 
tree to make that node placed at the root of the tree.
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Splaying
•When we access a node N, splaying is performed on N to move it to the root . To 
perform a splay operation, certain splay steps are performed where each step moves N 
closer to the root . 
•Splaying a particular node of interest after every access ensures that the recently 
accessed nodes are kept closer to the root and the tree remains roughly balanced, so 
that the desired amortized time bounds can be achieved .
•Each splay step depends on three factors :
✓Whether N is the left or right child of its parent P 
✓Whether P is the root or not, and if not 
✓Whether P is the left or right child of its parent G (N’s grandparent)
subject: data structures & algorithms

✓Step 1: Search N in the splay tree. If the search is successful, splay at the node N.
✓Step 2: If the search is unsuccessful, add the new node N in such a way that it 
replaces the NULL pointer reached during the search by a pointer to a new node

Searching for a Node in a Splay Tree
•If a particular node N is present in the splay tree then a pointer to the N is 
returned; otherwise a pointer to the null node is returned.
•The steps performed to search a node N in a splay tree includes:
✓Search down the root of the splay tree looking for N 
✓If the search is successful, and we reach N then splay the tree at N and return a pointer to N 
✓If the search is unsuccessful, i.e., the splay tree does not contain N, then we reach the null 
node. Splay the tree at the last non -null node reached during the search and return a pointer 
to null.

tree). Finally splay the tree at P .

text:
Tournament Bracket : Think of a heap tree as 
a tournament bracket where competitors 
(nodes) are ranked, and the winner (parent 
node) emerges from each match to proceed 
to the next round .
•In a max heap , the strongest competitor 
(highest value) always wins and stays at the top 
of the bracket . Each match ensures that the 
winner from the lower rounds must be stronger 
or equally strong compared to others beneath 
them .
•In a min heap , the weakest competitor (lowest 
value) rises to the top, and only competitors 
weaker than those below them remain at the 
top.
During each "round," competitors can "swap" 
based on their performance until the best (or 
worst, in the case of a min heap) competitor 
reaches the top.

# Python program for implementation of heap Sort
# To heapify subtree rooted at index i. n is size of heap
def heapify(arr, n, i):
largest = i # Initialize largest as root
l = 2 * i + 1 # left = 2* i + 1
r = 2 * i + 2 # right = 2* i + 2
# See if left child of root exists and is greater than root
if l < n and arr[i] < arr[l]:
largest = l
# See if right child of root exists and is greater than root
if r < n and arr[largest] < arr[r]:
largest = r
# Change root, if needed
if largest ! = i:
(arr[i], arr[largest]) = (arr[largest], arr[i]) # swap
# Heapify the root.
heapify(arr, n, largest)# The main function to sort an array of given size
def heapSort (arr):
n = len(arr)
# Build a maxheap.
# Since last parent will be at ((n//2) -1) we can start 
at that location.
for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
heapify(arr, n, i)
# One by one extract elements
for i in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
(arr[i], arr[0]) = (arr[0], arr[i]) # swap
heapify(arr, i, 0)

Priority Queue
•A priority queue is a special type of queue in which each element is associated with a priority value . And 
elements are served on the basis of their priority . That is, higher priority elements are served first .
•However, if elements with the same priority occur, they are served according to their order in the queue .
•Difference between Priority Queue and Normal Queue
•In a queue, the first -in-first -out rule is implemented whereas, in a priority queue, the values are removed on the basis of 
priority . The element with the highest priority is removed first .
•Implementation of Priority Queue
•Priority queue can be implemented using an array, a linked list, a heap data structure, or a binary search tree . Among 
these data structures, heap data structure provides an efficient implementation of priority queues .

text:
K Dimensional tree
•A K-D Tree (also called as K-Dimensional Tree ) is a binary search tree where data in each 
node is a K-Dimensional point in space . 
•In short, it is a space partitioning(details below) data structure for organizing points in a 
K-Dimensional space .
•A non-leaf node in K-D tree divides the space into two parts, called as half-spaces .
•Points to the left of this space are represented by the left subtree of that node and 
points to the right of the space are represented by the right subtree . 
•One of the primary advantages of K-D trees is that they allow for efficient k-nearest 
neighbor (KNN) queries , which are useful in applications such as image recognition and 
recommendation systems . 
•They can also be used for range queries, which allow for fast searches of points within a 
given radius or bounding box.
•We will soon be explaining the concept on how the space is divided and tree is formed .

Why Hashing ?
➢Fast Data Retrieval : Hashing enables O(1) average -time complexity for 
insert, search, and delete operations, making it essential for high-
performance applications .
➢Efficient Indexing in Databases : Hash tables are used in database indexing 
(e.g., hash-based indexing in DBMS) to improve query performance .
➢Optimized Memory Usage : Hashing reduces unnecessary memory usage by 
mapping data efficiently, avoiding excessive storage requirements .
➢Cryptographic Security : Hash functions play a crucial role in cryptography, 
securing passwords, digital signatures, and blockchain technology .
➢Load Balancing in Distributed Systems : Hashing is used in load balancing 
algorithms (e.g., consistent hashing in distributed databases and caching) .

text:
Why Hashing ?
➢Fast Keyword Lookup in AI/ML Applications : Used in Natural 
Language Processing (NLP) and information retrieval for indexing and 
searching massive text datasets efficiently .
➢Improves Data Deduplication : Hashing helps detect duplicate records 
in large datasets, reducing redundancy in AI/ML data pipelines .
➢Optimized Searching in AI and ML Algorithms : Hash tables speed up 
lookups in machine learning models, such as feature hashing in high-
dimensional datasets .
➢Collision Resolution for Better Data Integrity : Techniques like 
chaining, open addressing, and cuckoo hashing prevent hash collisions, 
ensuring data consistency .
➢Scalability in Big Data Processing : Hashing is fundamental in large-
scale data processing frameworks (e.g., MapReduce, Spark) to 
distribute workloads efficiently .

•Approach 1: Open addressing (Continued)

•Searches the hash table beginning with the original location that the hash function specifies and 
continues at increments of 12, 22, 32, and so on
•Possible problem
•Secondary clustering
•Double hashing 
•Uses two hash functions h1 and h2, where h2(key)  0 and h2  h1 
•Searches the hash table starting from the location that one hash function determines and considers 
every nth location, where n is determined from a second hash function
•Increasing the size of the hash table
•The hash function must be applied to every item in the old hash table before the item is placed 
into the new hash table

Example: Let us consider a simple hash function as “key mod 5” and a sequence 
of keys that are to be inserted are 50, 70, 76, 85, 93.
•Step1: First draw the empty hash table which will have a possible range of hash 
values from 0 to 4 according to the hash function provided.
•Step 2: Now insert all the keys in the hash table one by one. The first key is 50. 
It will map to slot number 0 because 50%5=0. So, insert it into slot number 0.
•Step 3: The next key is 70. It will map to slot number 0 because 70%5=0 but 50 
is already at slot number 0 so, search for the next empty slot and insert it.
•Step 4: The next key is 76. It will map to slot number 1 because 76%5=1 but 70 
is already at slot number 1 so, search for the next empty slot and insert it.
•Step 5: The next key is 93 It will map to slot number 3 because 93%5=3, So 
insert it into slot number 3.

text:
Quadratic Probing
•Tends to distribute keys better than linear probing
•Alleviates problem of clustering
•Runs the risk of an infinite loop on insertion, unless 
precautions are taken . 
–E.g., consider inserting the key 16 into a table of size 16, with 
positions 0, 1, 4 and 9 already occupied .
•When two keys hash to the same location, they will probe to the 
same alternative location . This may cause secondary clustering . 
•In order to avoid this secondary clustering, double hashing 
method is created where we use extra multiplications and 
divisions .

text:
Double Hashing
•Use a hash function
•Hash(key, i) = H1(key) + i * H2(key)
•Now the decrement is a function of the key
•The slots visited by the hash function will vary even if the initial slot 
was the same
•Avoids clustering
•Theoretically interesting, but in practice slower than quadratic probing, 
because of the need to evaluate a second hash function.
source: L13. Hash functions and hash tables.pdf
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Algorithms/ Procedure
•You must perform the following steps to find an empty slot:
1.Verify if hash1(key) is empty . If yes, then store the value on this 
slot.
2.If hash1(key) is not empty , then verify if hash1(key) + i * 
hash2(key) is empty . If yes, then store the value on this slot.
3.Keep incrementing the counter i and repeat until it finds an 
empty slot.

entries more uniformly.
•When R is not prime, or if it's a factor of the table size, it can lead to cyclic probing , 
never exploring some parts of the table.
•This risks infinite probing loops when inserting or searching.Why R Should Be Prime ?

•A good hash function should
•Be easy and fast to compute
•Scatter the data evenly throughout the hash table
•Issues to consider with regard to how evenly a hash function scatters the 
search keys
•How well does the hash function scatter random data?

REHASHING
•When the load factor exceeds a threshold, double the table size 
(smallest prime > 2 * old table size).
•Rehash each record in the old table into the new table.

•However, if the threshold is large (e.g., ½), then we need to rehash 
only once per O(N) insertions, so the cost is “amortized” constant -
time.

text:
Playlist Engine - Q&A with Answers
Q1 Why is a Doubly Linked List better than an Array for a playlist?
 Arrays require O(n) shifting when inserting or deleting in the middle. DLL performs O(1) insert/delete given 
a pointer to the node. Playlists constantly add/remove songs mid -list, so DLL is superior. Arrays only win for 
random access by index.
Q2 Why Circular DLL specifically - what does the circular property add?
 Circular DLL connects the tail's next → head and head's prev → tail. This gives seamless 'loop repeat' 
mode — after the last song, next() automatically returns to the first in O(1), without any special case code.
Q3 How would you implement the 'Shuffle' feature efficiently?
 Extract all node values into a Python list O(n), apply Fisher -Yates shuffle O(n), rebuild the circular DLL from 
shuffled values O(n). Total: O(n) time, O(n) space. In -place shuffling of a DLL is also possible by swapping 
node data fields.

Design Challenge: Which hash strategy + collision

MD5 / SHA hash of URL
+ Unique per URL
– 128 bits → too long, need to truncate → collisions
Base62 counter (auto -incr)
+ Simple, no collision
– Predictable sequential codes, security risk

text:
URL Shortener - Hashing Q&A with 
Answers
Q1 Why is O(1) lookup critical for a URL shortener's expand() operation?
 Every web redirect is a 302 HTTP response that must complete in < 10ms for good UX. At 100K 
redirects/sec, any O(n) or O(log n) lookup adds cumulative latency. Hash maps deliver O(1) average lookup — 
the only feasible choice at this scale.
Q2 What is Robin Hood Hashing and why is it preferred over basic linear probing?
 Robin Hood hashing is open addressing where during insertion, if the new key has travelled farther from its 
home slot than the resident key, they swap. This 'robs from rich, gives to poor' — it reduces variance in probe 
lengths, capping the max probe distance and keeping average lookup near O(1) even at 70% load.
Q3 How would you generate collision -free 6 -character short codes at scale?
 Strategy: Use MD5(longURL) → take first 6 Base62 chars. If collision: append a counter and rehash.

S O L U T I O N S
Case 1 — Linked List Homework Answers
HW1 Solution — CircularDLL Key Code
class Node:
def __init__(self, title): self.title = title; self.prev = self.next = None
class CircularDLL:
def __init__(self): self.head = None; self.size = 0
def add_song(self, title): # O(1) at head
node = Node(title)
if not self.head: node.next = node.prev = node; self.head = node
else: tail = self.head.prev # Circular: tail is head.prev
node.next=self.head; node.prev=tail; tail.next=node; self.head.prev=node
self.size += 1
def next_song(self): self.head = self.head.next # O(1) — just move head pointer
def prev_song(self): self.head = self.head.prev # O(1) — circular, no boundary check!
HW2 Solution — Reverse DLL in O(n), O(1)
def reverse(head):
curr = head
while curr:
curr.prev, curr.next = curr.next, curr.prev
curr = curr.prev # old next
return head.prev # new headHW3 Solution — Floyd's Cycle Detection

Hamiltonian Graph
•Hamiltonian path (also called traceable path) is a path that visits each 
vertex exactly once.
•A Hamiltonian cycle (also called Hamiltonian circuit , vertex tour or graph 
cycle) is a cycle that visits each vertex exactly once (except for the 
starting vertex, which is visited once at the start and once again at the 
end).
•A graph that contains a Hamiltonian path is called a traceable graph . 
A graph that contains a Hamiltonian cycle is called a Hamiltonian graph . 
Any Hamiltonian cycle can be converted to a Hamiltonian path by 
removing one of its edges, but a Hamiltonian path can be extended to 
Hamiltonian cycle only if its endpoints are adjacent .

text:
Euler Path and Euler Circuit (Cycle)
•Euler Path: A path that visits every edge exactly once .
•Euler Circuit (Cycle): A Euler Path that starts and ends at the same vertex.
Key Points :
•Can visit vertices multiple times, but each edge only once.
•Exists if:
•Euler Path: Exactly 0 or 2 vertices have odd degree.
•Euler Circuit: All vertices have even degree.
•Example : The classic Königsberg bridge problem is an Euler path problem.
•Hamiltonian Path and Hamiltonian Circuit (Cycle)
•Hamiltonian Path: A path that visits every vertex exactly once .
•Hamiltonian Circuit (Cycle): A Hamiltonian Path that starts and ends at the same vertex.
Key Points :
•Each vertex is visited exactly once.
•Edges can be reused as long as no vertex is repeated (except start = end in cycle).
•No simple rule for existence like Euler , it's an NP -complete problem.
•Example : The Traveling Salesman Problem is based on finding a minimum -cost Hamiltonian cycle.

Breadth -first traversal
Consider implementing a breadth -first traversal on a graph:
•Choose any vertex , mark it as visited and push it onto queue
•While the queue is not empty :
•Pop to top vertex vfrom the queue
•For each vertex adjacent to vthat has not been visited:
•Mark, it visited, and
•Push it onto the queue
This continues until the queue is empty
•Note: if there are no unvisited vertices, the graph is connected

text:
Why is it O(V + E) ?
Visiting Each Vertex: O(V)
•In BFS, each node is enqueued and dequeued exactly once .
•So, the total time spent on processing all the vertices is O(V) .
Traversing Each Edge: O(E)
•For each vertex, BFS looks at all of its adjacent neighbors (i.e., its edges).
•Over the entire algorithm, each edge is looked at once (in an undirected 
graph, twice, once from each side, but that still counts as O(E)).
•So, the total combined time is O(V + E)

Consider implementing a depth -first traversal on a graph :
•Choose any vertex, mark it as visited
•From that vertex :
•If there is another adjacent vertex not yet visited , go to it
•Otherwise, go back to the most previous vertex that has not yet had all of its 
adjacent vertices visited and continue from there
•Continue until no visited vertices have unvisited adjacent vertices
 Two implementations :

•Iterative

text:
Why is DFS O(V + E)?
Visiting Each Vertex: O(V)
•In DFS, each vertex is visited exactly once .
•When a vertex is visited, it is marked as visited and not revisited.
•So, the cost for visiting all vertices = O(V) .
Traversing Each Edge: O(E)
•For each visited vertex, DFS explores its adjacent vertices (edges).
•Each edge is visited once (or twice in an undirected graph) .
•Total time to go through all adjacency lists = O(E) .
So overall, time = O(V) + O(E) = O(V + E)

text:
Critical path
Suppose each task has a performance time associated with it
•If the tasks are performed serially, the time required to complete the 
last task equals to the sum of the individual task times
•These tasks require 0.3 + 0.7 + 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.1 = 2.0 s to execute serially
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Critical path
Suppose two tasks are ready to execute
•We could perform these tasks in parallel
•Computer tasks can be executed in parallel (multi -processing)
•Different tasks can be completed by different teams in a company
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Critical path
Suppose Task A completes
•We can now execute Tasks B and D in parallel
•However, Task E cannot execute until Task C completes, and Task C cannot 
execute until Task B completes
•The least time in which these five tasks can be completed is
 0.3 + 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.1 = 1.3 s
•This is called the critical time of all tasks
•The path (A, B, C, E) is said to be the critical path
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Critical path
The program described previously
shows the critical path in red
•We will define the critical time of each task 
to be the earliest time that it could be 
completed after the start of execution
Ref: The Standard Task Graph
 http://www.kasahara.elec.waseda.ac.jp/schedule/
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Finding the critical path
Tasks that have no prerequisites have a critical time equal to the time it 
takes to complete that task
 For tasks that depend on others, the critical time will be:
•The maximum critical time that it takes to complete a prerequisite 
•Plus the time it takes to complete this task
 In this example, the critical times are:
•Task A completes in 0.3 s
•Task B must wait for A and completes after 0.8 s
•Task D must wait for A and completes after 1.0 s
•Task C must wait for B and completes after 1.2 s
•Task E must wait for both C and D, and completes after
 max(1.0, 1.2) + 0.1 = 1.3 s
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Finding the critical path
Thus, we require more information:
•We must know the execution time of each task
•We will have to record the critical time for each task
•Initialize these to zero
•We will need to know the previous task with the longest critical time to 
determine the critical path
•Set these to null
subject: data structures & algorithms

Finding the critical path
Each time we pop a vertex v, in addition to what we 
already do:
•For v, add the task time onto the critical time for that vertex:
•That is the critical time for v
•For each adjacent vertex w:
•If the critical time for v is greater than the currently stored critical time 
for w
•Update the critical time with the critical time for v
•Set the previous pointer to the vertex v

ConnectMe, a growing social network, uses DFS to suggest new friends . Each user is a node ; a

Eve(E), Frank(F) . Edges : A–B, A–C, B–D, C–E, D–F. DFS from A visits B → D → F (backtrack) →

DFS explores depth -first, discovering 
indirect connections quickly without 
needing to process all immediate 
neighbors first. It uses a stack (O(V) 
memory), which is efficient when 
wide shallow BFS trees would 
consume excessive memory .

Stack (bottom→top) : [A, B, D]. A

How would you modify DFS to limit 
suggestions to 3 hops from Alice?

prunes the traversal at the 3-hop

Discussion
01 How does DFS handle disconnected graphs, and what changes are needed in the algorithm?
Standard DFS only visits nodes reachable from the start vertex . For disconnected graphs, you must loop 
through all vertices and call DFS on any that remain unvisited . This ensures all components are 
explored . The outer loop adds O(V) overhead but ensures completeness .
02How DFS can detect cycles in a directed graph. What additional tracking is required?
Use two sets: 'visited' (ever seen) and 'in-stack' (currently in recursion path) . When DFS visits a node 
already in-stack, a back -edge exists, indicating a cycle . This is distinct from undirected cycle 
detection, which only needs the visited set plus parent tracking .

A cashier wants to give change using the fewest number of coins . They

possible candidate solutions for the problem .
•It is a generic method and not limited to any specific domain of problems .
•The brute force method is ideal for solving small and simpler problems .

•The brute force approach is inefficient . For real-time problems, algorithm analysis often goes 
above the O(N!) order of growth .

than on a good algorithm design . Brute force algorithms are slow.

Implementation and analysis
The initialization requires (|V|) memory and run time
 We iterate |V| – 1 times, each time finding the closest vertex
•Iterating through the table requires is (|V|) time
•Each time we find a vertex, we must check all of its neighbors
•With an adjacency matrix, the run time is (|V|(|V| + |V|)) = (|V|2)
•With an adjacency list, the run time is (|V|2 + |E|) = (|V|2) as |E| = O(| V|2)
 Can we do better?
•Recall, we only need the shortest edge next
•How about a priority queue?
•Assume we are using a binary heap
•We will have to update the heap structure —this requires additional work

text:
Implementation and analysis
The initialization still requires (|V|) memory and run time
•The priority queue will also requires (|V|) memory
 We iterate |V| – 1 times, each time finding the closest vertex
•Place the shortest distances into a priority queue
•The size of the priority queue is (|V|)
•Thus, the work required for this is O(|V| ln(|V|))
 Is this all the work that is necessary?
•Recall that each edge visited may result in a new edge being pushed to the 
very top of the heap
•Thus, the work required for this is O(|E| ln(|V|))
 Thus, the total run time is O(|V| ln(|V|) + |E| ln(|V|)) = O(|E| ln(|V|))

Kruskal’s algorithm
Finding a minimum spanning treeImagine you are forming a friendship network in a school, where students (nodes) need to 
be connected with the least possible effort (minimum cost) . Each friendship (edge) has a 
different strength (weight), and your goal is to form the strongest network with minimal 
effort while ensuring everyone is connected .
How do you do it?
1.Start by identifying the strongest friendships (edges with the lowest weight) .
2.Connect the students one by one, always choosing the strongest remaining friendship 
that does not create a cycle .
3.Continue until all students are connected in a way that minimizes the total effort .
This is exactly how Kruskal’s Algorithm works —by sorting edges in increasing order of 
weight and adding them one by one, ensuring that no cycles are formed, until a Minimum 
Spanning Tree (MST) is built .

minimum spanning trees on all connected sub -graphs

Prim’s vs. Kruskal’s Algorithm – A Real -World 
Comparison
Prim’s Algorithm – Expanding a City’s Power Grid 
Imagine you are expanding an electric power grid in a city. You start from one 
power station and extend connections step by step to the nearest location, 
ensuring minimum cost at each step . Prim’s Algorithm grows like this—
expanding from a starting node, always choosing the nearest connection .
Kruskal’s Algorithm – Building a Road Network 
Now, think of constructing a road network between multiple cities . You sort all 
possible roads by cost and pick the cheapest ones first, ensuring all cities are 
connected without forming loops . Kruskal’s Algorithm works this way—starting 
with the smallest edges and connecting components gradually .
Key Difference :
•Prim’s works node by node , like growing a tree from a starting point .
•Kruskal’s works edge by edge , like choosing the best roads first to form the 
network .

Questions:
•What if at some point, all unvisited vertices have a distance ∞?

subgraph containing the source vertex 
•What if we just want to find the shortest path between vertices 
vj and vk?
Apply the same algorithm, but stop when we are visiting vertex vk
•Does the algorithm change if we have a directed graph?
No

text:
Implementation and analysis
The initialization still requires Q(| V|) memory and run time
•The priority queue will also require O(| V|) memory
•We must use an adjacency list, not an adjacency matrix
 We iterate | V| times, each time finding the closest vertex to the source
•Place the distances into a priority queue
•The size of the priority queue is O(| V|)
•Thus, the work required for this is O(| V| ln(|V|))
 Is this all the work that is necessary?
•Recall that each edge visited may result in a new edge being pushed 
to the very top of the heap
•Thus, the work required for this is O(| E| ln(|V|))
 Thus, the total run time is O(| V| ln(|V|) + | E| ln(|V|)) = O(| E| ln(|V|))

text:
Bellman -Ford Algorithm Limitations :
1.Slower Runtime : It has a time complexity of O(V × E), making it inefficient 
for large graphs .
2.Not Suitable for Dense Graphs : Performs poorly when the number of 
edges is very high.
3.Inefficient Compared to Dijkstra : Though it handles negative weights, it’s 
slower than Dijkstra’s for graphs with only positive weights .Dijkstra’s Algorithm Limitations:
1.No Negative Weights : Cannot handle graphs with negative edge weights , 
as it may produce incorrect results.
2.Depends on Priority Queue : The performance heavily relies on the data 
structure used (e.g., binary heap or Fibonacci heap).
3.May Not Be Optimal in Certain Scenarios : For dynamic graphs or when 
real-time updates are needed, it’s not ideal without modifications.

text:
Imagine you're navigating a city using a GPS .
You want to reach your destination as quickly as 
possible ; so, your GPS not only considers the 
distance you've already traveled (like Dijkstra’s 
algorithm) but also estimates how far you still 
have to go using a straight -line distance 
(heuristic) .
 In A*:
•The actual cost so far = time or distance you've 
already driven .
•The estimated cost to goal = the GPS's guess 
of how far you still need to go.
•A* chooses the path that looks most promising 
overall , combining both!
•It's like a smart traveler who doesn’t just blindly 
follow roads - but also thinks ahead .
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
A* search
•A* Search is an informed pathfinding algorithm that combines the cost to reach a 
node (g(n)) with a heuristic estimate (h(n)) of the cost to reach the goal .
•It selects the path with the lowest total estimated cost (f(n) = g(n) + h(n)), 
balancing exploration and goal -directed search .
•Widely used in GPS navigation and AI planning, A* guarantees the shortest path if 
the heuristic is admissible .“Best First Greedy ” heuristic search
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
Outline
In this topic, we will look at the A* search algorithm:
•It solves the single -source shortest path problem
•Restricted to physical environments
•First described in 1968 by Peter Hart, Nils Nilsson, and Bertram Raphael
•Similar to Dijkstra’s algorithm
•Uses a hypothetical shortest distance to weight the paths
subject: data structures & algorithms

text:
A* Algorithm works as -
A* Algorithm works as -
•It maintains a tree of paths originating at the start node .
•It extends those paths one edge at a time .
•It continues until its termination criterion is satisfied .
A* Algorithm extends the path that minimizes the following function -
f(n) = g(n) + h(n)
Here,
•‘n’ is the last node on the path
•g(n) is the cost of the path from start node to node ‘n’
•h(n) is a heuristic function that estimates cost of the cheapest path from node ‘n’ to the 
goal node

text:
Algorithm
•The implementation of A* Algorithm involves 
maintaining two lists- OPEN and CLOSED .
•OPEN contains those nodes that have been 
evaluated by the heuristic function but have 
not been expanded into successors yet.
•CLOSED contains those nodes that have 
already been visited .
The algorithm is as follows -
Step-01:
•Define a list OPEN .
•Initially, OPEN consists solely of a 
single node, the start node S.
Step-02:
•If the list is empty, return failure and 
exit.Step -03:
•Remove node n with the smallest value of f(n) 
from OPEN and move it to list CLOSED .
•If node n is a goal state, return success and exit.
Step -04:
•Expand node n.
Step -05:
• If any successor to n is the goal node, return 
success and the solution by tracing the path 
from goal node to S.
•Otherwise, go to Step -06.
Step -06:
• For each successor node,
•Apply the evaluation function f to the node .
•If the node has not been in either list, add it to 
OPEN .
Step -07:
• Go back to Step -02.

A* uses an admissible heuristic (straight -line distance) to guide the

Q3What makes a graph bipartite, and how is it 
detected?
A graph is bipartite if its vertices can be split into two disjoint sets 
such that every edge crosses between sets (no edge within a set). 
BFS-based 2-coloring detects this: assign color 0 to source, color 1 
to all neighbors, recurse . If any neighbor has the same color as the 
current node, the graph contains an odd cycle and is NOT bipartite .

Q1Why does Kruskal's algorithm produce an optimal 
(minimum cost) spanning tree?
Kruskal's is a greedy algorithm that exploits the Cut Property : the 
minimum -weight edge crossing any cut of the graph belongs to 
some MST . By sorting edges and greedily adding the cheapest 
edge that doesn't form a cycle, it assembles the globally optimal 
spanning tree. Correctness follows from the greedy exchange 
argument .
Q2When would you prefer Prim's over Kruskal's 
algorithm?
Prim's is preferred for dense graphs (E close to V²) because its 
adjacency matrix version runs in O(V²), matching or beating 
Kruskal's O(E log E) for dense graphs . Prim's also naturally 
extends to incremental updates (adding one node to an existing
subject: data structures & algorithms

extends to incremental updates (adding one node to an existing 
MST), while Kruskal's would need a full re-sort.
Q3How does Union -Find (DSU) enable cycle detection in 
Kruskal's?
Each node starts in its own set. Before adding edge (u,v), Find(u) 
and Find(v) check their roots . If both share the same root, 
adding the edge would create a cycle - so it's skipped . 
Otherwise, Union(u,v) merges their sets. With union by rank 
and path compression, each Find is nearly O(1) amortized 
(inverse Ackermann time) .

Uber must pre-compute travel times between all zones in a

min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]) for all intermediate nodes 
k. The resulting distance matrix powers surge zone 
calculation and driver ETA estimation . For real-time dispatch, 
a greedy matching algorithm (assign nearest available driver 
using the pre-computed matrix) runs in O(D) per request (D

Q1Explain the Floyd -Warshall recurrence and why it is a 
Dynamic Programming algorithm.
dist[i][j][k] = min(dist[i][j][k -1], dist[i][k][k -1] + dist[k][j][k -1]). It 
builds optimal solutions from sub-problems : the shortest path 
using only nodes 1..k is either the path using only 1..k-1, or the 
path through node k. Optimal substructure and overlapping 
subproblems make it a classic DP. Space is optimised to O(V²) by 
updating in-place .
Q2How does Floyd -Warshall detect negative -weight 
cycles?
After running the algorithm, inspect the main diagonal : if dist[i][i] 
< 0 for any vertex i, the graph contains a negative -weight cycle 
reachable through i. This is because a path from i back to i via a

Q3Why is topological sort needed, and when does it fail?
Topological sort produces a linear ordering of vertices in a DAG such 
that for every edge (u→v), u appears before v. It's used to schedule 
tasks with dependencies (e.g., zone updates, build systems) . It fails - 
and no ordering exists - if and only if the graph contains a directed 
cycle (detected by DFS via back -edge identification) .

Problem 1 [10 points] 
What is the difference between the following? Be precise. Give examples where possible. 

(a) Bias vs. Variance 
- Bias defines the complexity of the model – the distance between the ideal model and the 
average model given the size of the search space. 
- Variance defines the ability to find the model within the search space – the larger the 
search space, the lower is the probability of finding the right model – variance increases
subject: machine learning ii

text:
(b) 1-vs-Rest Classifier vs. Pair-wise Classifier 
- 1-vs-rest classifier: Breaks the C > 2 class problem into C 2-class problems where it 
takes one of the classes as target (positive) and all others (rest) as negative. 
- Pair-wise classifier: Breaks the C > 2 class problem in C-choose-2 2-class problems and 
learns a classifier for each unique class pair. 

(c) Bagging vs. Boosting 
- Bagging: builds a number of weak classifiers by either sampling the data or by sampling 
the feature and aggregates the outputs of these classifiers. 
- Boosting: iteratively builds the next model by increasing the weights of data points that 
were not doing well on the cumulative model so far.
subject: machine learning ii

text:
(d) SVM Kernel Trick 2 vs. SVM Kernel Trick 3 
- SVM Kernel Trick 2: addresses the noise problem in the data by introducing slack 
variables and the C parameter to play with model complexity. 
- SVM Kernel Trick 3: addresses the non-linearity problem in the data by introducing non- 
linear kernels to bend the space and build linear models in the bent space. 

(e) Perceptron Classifier vs. Linear SVM Classifier 
- Perceptron Classifiers: mimic how the neurons learn by updating the weights on the 
next example if it is on the wrong side. Non-deterministic, sub-optimal, not noise robust. 
- Linear SVM Classifier: maximum margin classifiers that learn a unique (deterministic),
subject: machine learning ii

text:
noise-robust linear boundary between classes using a quadratic programming. 

(f) Linear Discriminant Analysis vs. Quadratic Discriminant Analysis 
- Linear Discriminant Analysis: Model linear decision boundary because they assume the 
two Bayesians for the two classes to have the same covariance matrix. 
- Quadratic Discriminant Analysis: Model quadratic decision boundary because they 
assume two Bayesians with two different covariance matrices per class.
subject: machine learning ii

text:
(g) Linear Models vs. Generalized Linear Models 
- Linear Model: Directly models the expected output as a linear combination of the inputs: 
𝐸[𝑌∣𝑋] =𝛽଴+𝛽்𝑋 
Use the raw input as the features directly and learn a linear model in the original space. 
- Generalized Linear Model: Keeps the inputs linear, but uses a link function to connect that 
linear expression to the expected output: 
𝑔(𝐸[𝑌∣𝑋]) =𝛽଴+𝛽்𝑋 
Example: linear regression is a linear model, while logistic regression is a generalized linear 
model. First transform the input space into another space by applying any number of non-linear 
transformations and then learn a linear model in that space.
subject: machine learning ii

text:
(h) Induction in Bayesian Networks vs. Deduction in Bayesian Networks 
- Deduction in Bayesian Networks 
Reasoning forward along the arrows: given the CAUSE, infer the EFFECT. You apply the network's 
CPTs (the known rules) to propagate evidence from parents down to children. Also called 
predictive or causal reasoning. 
- Induction in Bayesian Networks 
Reasoning backward against the arrows: given the EFFECT, infer the CAUSE. You observe a child 
node and use Bayes' theorem to update belief over its parents. Also called diagnostic or 
evidential reasoning (strictly, abduction). 

(i) Pair-wise Classifiers vs. Binary Hierarchical Classifiers 
- Pairwise Classifiers: Learn a classifier for each pair of classes – total C-choose-2 
- Binary Hierarchical: Learns a binary tree of classifiers by merging bottom up the most 
similar classes together like in agglomerative clustering – C-1 2-class classifiers.
subject: machine learning ii

text:
(j) Decision Trees vs. Random Forest 
- Decision Tree: A classification method that greedily partitions the input space into pure 
regions by picking the next best variable to partition by in any region or part of the tree. 
- Random Forrest: Bagging applied to Decision trees (weak) by training many trees with 
randomly sampled feature spaces and then aggregating their outputs.

We are claiming that any matrix ‘A’ (square or rectangular, weather full set of eigen vectors exist or not) can be factorized
If A is a matrix with full set of eigen vectors, then we put the independent eigen vectors as columns of a matrix ‘S’. We def ine a 
diagonal matrix Λ that contains the eigen values of ‘A’ as the diagonal elements. Since, S is made of independent eigen vectors, 
we can always find S−1. We can then factorize the matrix A as A=SΛS−1. On top of that, if ‘A’ happens to be symmetric, then 
we know for sure that the eigen values of A will always be real and the eigen vectors will be orthogonal. We can always 
normalize orthonormal eigen vectors to obtain orthonormal eigen vectors. In that special situation, S will be an orthonormal 
matrix. A special property of orthonormal matrices is that S−1=ST. A symmetric matrix can therefore be factorized into 
SΛST, thereby saving us 1 additional computation step of calculating the inverse of S.

multiplication by a scalar and addition of vectors . Meaning, if I multiply a vector by a scalar, the resultant vector must still be 
inside that space, or, if I take two vectors and add them, the resultant vector would still be inside that space . So, only if my 
space containing the vectors satisfies the criterion of being closed under linear combination (scalar multiplication and 
addition), can I call it a vector space, or else not.Two very important algebraic operations that we do to vectors : scalar multiplication and vector addition, jointly called taking 
linear combinations .

Why is RREF useful computationally?
Because RREF tells you everything important about a system in one glance: what’s solvable, what’s redundant, what’s free, and 
what actually matters.
•Feature selection / multicollinearity
•Linear regression (core ML model)
•Underdetermined systems (common in ML)
•Neural networks (hidden layer redundancy)
Every time you remove redundant features, solve regression, or 
deal with underdetermined systems, you are using RREF, whether 
you see it or not

The normal equation ATAොx=ATb becomes QTQොx=QTb.

Since Ax=λx, we look at the equation A−λIx=0.

The trivial solution would be x=0. We are not interested in this trivial solution. This would mean, any and every eigen vector 
of the matrix is the zero -vector.

Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive foundation in linear algebra with a focus on applications in AI and data science. Students will explore vector spaces, matrix operations, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and transformations that form the mathematical basis for numerous AI algorithms. The course emphasizes computational techniques and practical implementation through Python programming, enabling students to develop a robust understanding of how linear algebraic concepts underpin modern machine learning methods including dimensionality reduction, principal component analysis, and neural networks.

Apply matrix operations and decompositions to solve systems of linear equations

Summary of Session

Categorical variables can be included by creating binary/dummy variables in regression

For m categories, you need m-1 dummy variables and the remaining one acts as a reference or control category

Coefficients of categorical variables capture the average difference in the response variable between the category of interest and the reference category
Interaction between categorical and numerical variables can be modeled by calculating a new variable that is product of the two variables
Interaction captures the difference in association between the response variable and the numerical variable for different categories

Let’s say that the manager is a relaxed personality, so he says as long as the mean call duration is between 2 and 6 minutes, I am not going to bother. On the other hand someone else is very cautious and says, I will stop everytime the mean goes beyond 3 and 5. Which one is better?

text:
The size of the band does not depend on the variability data as much as it does on the consequences. There are two kinds of mistakes you can make here in disentangling the variability. You can be alarmed because of one bad sample even when the process is fine (this is type I error). You go to the doctor but it is just a bad case of common cold. On the other hand, you might have a wide tolerance band and don’t go to the doctor although you have a severe case of bronchitis (this is type II error). Where you draw the line depends on the cost of interrupting your routine and visiting the doctor now vs. cost of treating a severe ailment later. So on one hand, there is cost of investigation and on the other cost of changed process. 

In most cases, people have a target of type I error – nobody wants to unnecessarily interrupt the process, people believe problems come rarely.

text:
Assumptions of Multiple Regression
All the assumptions of the SLR model are required
Linear specification is correct: Y = β0 + β1X + ε
Errors are uncorrelated with explanatory variables: E[ε|X] = 0
Constant variance of errors: Var[εi]= σε2
Errors are independent of each other: Corr[εi, εj] = 0
Error term is normally distributed: εi ~ N (0, σε2)

In addition, no predictor variable should be a linear combination of other predictor variables – no multicollinearity
e.g. We do not want the situation like: X2 = 3X1 + 7.2X3 – 0.54X4
Here, if we regress X2 against X1, X3, X4 we will get R2 = 1
All variation in X2 is explained by other variables

Notes: This is one of the fundamental results of statistics and it has immense practical value. Almost the entire methodology that we are going to develop in this course, all software programs use this theorem on a routine basis. It says that the distribution of the sample mean is normal if the data is normally distributed. But even if the data is not normally distributed but you take a large enough sample and samples are drawn independently, the sample mean distribution is approximately normal. It also tells us that the mean of this distribution of sample means is the population mean and the standard deviation is population standard deviation divided by square root of the sample size.

Correlation is dimensionless - it is standardized using standard deviations
It always takes a value between -1 and 1
Close to +1 implies a linear relationship with a positive slope
Close to -1 implies a linear relationship with a negative slope
Close to 0 implies that there is no linear relationship

text: There are a fewthings we need to be aware of. First, that correlation cannot be used for predictive purposes. The other is the possibility of lurking variables. You see an association, which is not causation. Let me give you two examples – height and hair length. If I were to get these numbers for a random sample in India, what do you think we will see? A negative correlation. Does this mean that greater height reduces the hair length? Is there a biological reason for it? No, it is just that the gender has not been considered here, which is the lurking variable. Men tend to be longer than women in India and they also tend to keep shorter hair. Lastly, correlation is only pairwise. What if I wanted a framework that could be extended to multiple variables at the same time, especially when I put back the lurking variable? For this purpose, we look for framework that is more general.

Mr. Ram Kumar, a fresh graduate from Indian Institute of Management, Bangalore, had joined the corporate headquarters of United Technologies of India (UTI) a month ago. Other Incomes (OTINC.), as a percentage of PBT had increased from 6% to 65%. Personnel (EMPL) and Interest payment (INT) had both shot up. Ram wondered about the contribution of the different variables to Sales and PBT.

He felt that there were some reasons for concern. With his scientific background, he felt that any re-examination of corporate strategies must include analysis of past data. He decided to write a statistical report based on the available data.

Company Background

In the late sixties, the Indian government realized that the country lacked a sound manufacturing base in electronics. All vital components in Defense and Communication were being imported. The Indian government established UTI in 1971 to meet the national needs in every vital area of technology. Its customers were to include Defense, Department of Telecommunication, Department of Space and All India Radio.

text:
To acquire a sound manufacturing base, the company, in its early years, tied up with internationally reputed companies under know-how/license agreements. This helped the company to assimilate production technologies quickly and be capable of manufacturing a variety of products of international quality standards. While acquiring a viable manufacturing base, it also established its commitment to R&D by locating a laboratory in South India and investing 7% of the annual turnover in research. As a result, 75% of its business comes from products of indigenous design.

In the first decade, the company saw a steady growth due to the license agreements. There was a small hiccup in one year because of conflict between management and labour. In the eighties, there was a small boom in the country. Demand in the defense sector and in consumer electronics picked up. The company seized the opportunity and expanded. The investments in R&D paid off.

text:

But, in the recent times, UTI has come under pressure because of the new policies of the government. The ministry has been hinting about a cut in budgetary support and has been pushing the company to raise capital in the market.

Ever since its inception in 1971, UTI has been committed to meeting the national needs in every vital area of technology. And it strives to gain a reputation in Quality, Technology and Innovation.

text:
Note on Revert.
Git creates a new commit that represents the
inverse of the changes introduced by the specified
commit. In other words, Git applies the "inverse
patch" of the specified commit to the current
branch, effectively undoing the changes made by
that commit.

text:
How
git reset --hard [commit]
Works ?
subject: python programming

text:
Step-1
You specify the commit you want to reset to by
providing its identifier (commit hash) as an
argument to the git reset --hard command
subject: python programming

text:
Step-2
Git moves the HEAD pointer (the reference to the
current commit) to the specified commit
subject: python programming

text:
Step-3
Git resets the staging area and working directory to match
the state of the specified commit. This means that any
changes in the staging area or working directory that are
not part of the specified commit will be discarded.
subject: python programming

text:
Step-4
Any commits made after the specified commit, along with
their associated changes, are effectively removed from the
branch's history.

Given a data structure, some of the most fundamental operations we

# Note on Functions vs Methods in Python 

### Functions 
- Functions are a reusable unit of code 
- We can call functions using their name `<function_name>` and parenthesis `()`
- Functions can take any data and return the computed result. 

### Methods 
- Methods are like functions as they're also a reusable unit of code
- They're called on a particular data structure / object 
- Methods run in the scope of the data structure on which they're called 
- We can call methods as: `object_name`.`function_name`()
- Methods have access to the data of their parent object
